Case 1. The patient is a 34-year-old woman who has had symp­
toms consistent with SMS for more than 12 years but was diag­
nosed only recently (approximately 1 year ago) with it. The pa­
tient was treated with plasmapheresis and cyclophosphamide. 
She had two courses of plasmapheresis with symptomatic relief 
of her muscle spasms for approximately 2 months. Each course 
consisted of approximately six exchanges. The patient was re­
ferred from the neurology outpatient unit because of her GI com­
plaints. Her main complaint was constipation. She had some up­
per GI symptoms that included nausea, early satiety, and mild 
reflux symptoms. In addition, she had pharyngeal dysphagia, an 
intermittent hold-up of food in the pharynx. Abdominal films

showed no evidence of bowel dilation. The results of an anorectal 
motility study were normal-negative for sphincteric function. A 
gastric-emptying study using an isotope-labeled solid meal 
(chicken liver and beef stew) showed delayed gastric emptying. 
The time it took to empty 50% of the meal (T%) was 221 minutes. 
The percentage of solids retained at 120 minutes was 76% (normal 
values for T % and percent of retention at 2 hours are respectively, 
<150 minutes and <70%). An upper GI endoscopy and esopha­
geal motility study were not performed because of her painful 
muscle spasms secondary to SMS. Organic lesions, which can 
cause delayed gastric emptying, were excluded by barium studies. 
She had hypothyroidism that was controlled with hormone re­
placement. 
The patient began therapy with a prokinetic agent (10 mg cisa­
pride four times a day). In addition, 1 oz magnesium citrate daily 
was given to ease constipation. The patient was followed up for 
approximately 1 year. During the follow-up period, she continued 
to take cisapride 10 mg four times a day to increase motility 
throughout the gut and metoclopramide for nausea. The patient 
continued to have some degree of breakthrough nausea and vom­
iting approximately once or twice a week. Overall her weight was 
stable.

Figure 1. Esophageal motility tracing with the top four leads 
spaced 5 cm apart in the body of the esophagus, one lead in the 
lower esophageal sphincter and the lowest lead is in the stomach. 
All are constantly perfused by a pneumohydraulic system. Three 
wet swallows are represented and indicate both peristaltic and 
nonperistaltic contractions are occurring. The amplitude of the 
contractions is lower in the proximal two leads. The pressure 
in the lower esophageal sphincter was <10 mm Hg and hence 
decreased with normal swallow-induced relaxations.
